extractions.quote: Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare disorder of motor function characterized by progressive involuntary stiffness of muscles and superimposed painful spasms, which are often precipitated by startle, emotional, and tactile stimuli and movements of affected or unaffected muscles. SPS predominantly affects the trunk and proximal limb muscles’; however, unusual symptoms and signs such as involvement of distal or faciobulbar muscles and autonomic disturbances have been rep~rted.~,~ The pathogenesis of SPS is unclear. Evidence for a role of autoimmune mechanisms has been derived from the detection of autoantibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) in serum and CSF of 60% of SPS cases4 as well as from the observation of SPS in patients with a variety of malignant tumors, suggesting a paraneoplastic nature of SPS in these ~ases.~-~ Treatment of SPS has been mainly symptomatic. Several authors have reported beneficial effects from immunotherapeutic approache~.~.~.~ We report an atypical case of SPS with spinal MRI findings and autoantibodies against amphiphysin but without development of a malignancy in a GAD antibody-negative patient who markedly improved with methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide pulse therapy.

Therefore, we added methylprednisolone (MP) 1,000 mg iv for 3 days, followed by 80 mg po. Rigidity and pain were markedly reduced and spasms disappeared within a few days. However, reduction of MP below 60 mg led to a severe relapse. As intravenous immunoglobulins (IG, 30 g iv on 5 subsequent days) had no major effects until 9 days after the last infusion, an intravenous cyclophosphamide (CyP) pulse therapy was introduced (day 1: CyP 800 mg + MP 500 mg; days 2 and 3: MP 500 mg). This scheme, which began 8 months after onset of symptoms and was repeated seven times monthly, allowed subsequent reduction of oral MP and benzodiazepines.
